episodes.214677: During the morning hours of August 5th, a small line of storms brought widespread 60 to 80 mph winds to portions of Mercer, Putnam, Sullivan, and Adair Counties. The strongest winds and worst damage occurred across NE Mercer County and Putnam County. The town of Unionville sustained heavy damage, with tree limbs and power poles down all across town, making roads impassable and leading to widespread power outages. Barns and outbuildings were destroyed.
episodes.214686: A frontal boundary advanced through northeastern NM and washed up to the east slopes of the central mountain chain during the morning of August 4th. Daily rounds of afternoon thunderstorms were able to develop along the mountain chain August 4th through 6th, with several producing large or accumulating hail over portions of northeastern and central NM. One storm produced large hail over Philmont Scout Ranch on the 4th, with another producing severe hail near Folsom on the 5th, and a third producing accumulating hail and minor flooding impacts along NM3 just north of Encino, NM on the 6th. Additionally, a landspout was observed by a driver on Interstate 25 near Wagon Mound along the leading edge of an approaching severe warned thunderstorm on August 5th. Shower and thunderstorm activity dissipated during the evening hours each day.
episodes.214851: Isolated diurnally induced thunderstorms developed in an environment with precipitable water values around 1.8-2.0 inches and moderate instability. A cluster of storms that moved into the Columbia Metro area produced a downburst in the Lexington area.
episodes.214955: Thunderstorms impacted portions of southwest Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of August 5, 2026. These thunderstorms produced heavy rain which caused flooding of several roadways in the Lawrenceburg area, rendering them impassable.
episodes.216208: An area of low pressure tracked along a stationary front and produced flash flooding.
episodes.216211: An area of low pressure tracked along a stationary front and produced flash flooding.
episodes.216231: On the morning of August 5th, scattered showers were ongoing along the mountains of West Virginia, while a warm front lifted north through the area. More robust showers and thunderstorms developed in southeast Ohio and then progressed east across West Virginia as the decaying boundary was redirected across the area that afternoon into the night. Heavy downpours in thunderstorms deposited one to three inches of rain across portions of the state, which prompted instances of flooding in Kanawha and Upshur Counties. Primary impacts included flooding of a few roads and low spots.
episodes.216466: A stalled frontal boundary and area of low pressure over the southeastern United States produced widespread showers and embedded storms during the afternoon and evening hours. A single storm brought isolated flash flooding in Stanly County.
episodes.216572: A cluster of showers and thunderstorms produced a few wind gusts in excess of 34 knots from Saint George Island to Apalachee Bay.  In addition, waterspouts were reported offshore of Mexico Beach and Tyndall AFB.
episodes.217010: Slow moving thunderstorms dumped heavy rainfall across Bay county and resulted in flash flooding.  In addition, scattered afternoon and evening thunderstorms produced sporadic wind damage across the area.
episodes.217375: A closed upper level low was located across interior portions of the Southeast on August 4. This helped create widespread showers and storms in the vicinity of a stationary front draped across portions of south-central and southeastern Virginia. Given a tropical airmass in place with very high precipitable water values of 2-2.4 inches and high humidity, showers and storms were slow-movers and created very heavy rainfall rates. This resulted in heavy rain and flash flooding.
episodes.217706: A stalled frontal boundary to the northwest of the region, combined with the usual late summer daytime heating/influences of sea breezes, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the area. Precipitable Water (PWAT) values reached as high as 2.2 to 2.5 inches during this period, which strongly supported heavy rain and flooding potential.
episodes.217837: Just after midnight CST on the 4th a severe thunderstorm moved into the far northwest corner of Cimarron County. The storm quickly died with the decaying thunderstorm likely causing a heat burst that created wind gusts in the 58 to 62 mph range and lasted for about 5 minutes. |On the evening of the 5th more thunderstorms formed off the higher terrain in NM/CO and moved into Cimarron County. This time one of the storms maintained its strength and produced 1 hail near Kenton, OK.
episodes.217844: A stationary frontal boundary served as a focus for diurnally-driven thunderstorms over central and eastern Kentucky beginning during the late morning of August 5th, and lingering into the evening. While wind shear was weak, 1500-2500 J/kg of MLCAPE proved sufficient for briefly strong storms that produced a couple instances of wind damage via wet downbursts. In addition, the richly moist environment favored locally heavy rainfall with training storms which resulted in an instance of flash flooding near Lexington, where MRMS-estimated rainfall was over 4 inches.
episodes.217932: Deep moisture convergence along with modest instability and southerly flow supported widespread showers and thunderstorms capable of producing waterspouts across coastal waters.
episodes.218093: Slow-moving showers and thunderstorms created isolated flooding in areas. MRMS depicts 2 to 4 inches per hour rainfall rates in some areas.
episodes.218165: On the afternoon on August 5th, an isolated thunderstorm developed in southern Caddo Parish during peak heating with very hot and humid conditions as temperatures rose into the mid to upper 90s. Steering flow aloft was very weak so the thunderstorm sat nearly stationary until it produced a localized downburst directly over the Shreveport Regional Airport. As a result, damaging wind gusts in excess of 60 mph were recorded on multiple occasions by the automated weather sensor equipment located along the airfield property.
episodes.218221: Scattered storms developed across southeast Texas and one produced isolated flooding in Orange County.
episodes.218333: An elongated upper high extended across central New Mexico with moisture coming around from the northeast.  Slow moving storms produced flash flooding around Redrock and a severe wind gust in Hidalgo county.
episodes.218376: A period of persistent, heavy rainfall impacted the Susitna Valley in early August 2026, leading to excessive runoff and rapidly rising rivers. This resulted in moderate flooding across both the Western and Central Susitna Valley. The most severe impacts were concentrated along the Yentna River basin, where Lake Creek surged to its second-highest crest on record, forcing emergency evacuations of local wilderness lodges. Simultaneously, heavy rainfall overwhelmed local creeks and drainage infrastructure in the Petersville area, resulting in inundated roadways and washed-out culverts, while rapid rises on Moose Creek sent overland flow spilling across Oilwell Road. Further downstream, increased flows exacerbated riverbank erosion along the Skwentna River.
episodes.218498: Thunderstorms producing downpours resulted in flash flooding across New Jersey. Multiple cars were stuck in flood waters along with multiple water rescues.
episodes.218583: The active monsoon period continues with strong to severe thunderstorms, with the strongest storm in Douglas, AZ. The locally heavy rainfall led to multiple road closures and washed out a bridge with a car on it with no injuries reported.

A social media video showed deep flooding across the wide, low-lying mouth of Redrock Canyon just before the Gila River.  Flooding made roads north and west of the Gila River Bridge on Game Department Road impassable.  Most of the rain fell well upstream of the area.

Excessive rainfall totaling between 1.5 and 3 inches resulted in moderate flooding on the Yentna River at Lake Creek. The river initially reached moderate flood stage on August 4 at 4:50 PM AKDT, and continued to rise until it reached a crest of 22.45 feet on August 5 at 9:50 AM AKDT. This marked the second-highest crest on record for this location. This rise forced Wilderness Place Lodge to fully evacuate both guests and staffs. Floodwaters encroached upon several lodge buildings and cabins in the area. |Farther upstream, an observer on the Skwentna River reported significant riverbank erosion on August 6, noting that the river was rapidly eroding into the sandbank at the local boat launch.
